articles.title: ठंड की गिरफ्त में मध्य प्रदेश, दिवाली के बाद 360 डिग्री बदलेगा मौसम, रात में गिर रहा तापमान - ETV Bharat
articles.search_term: ("पारा चढ़ा" OR "पारा पहुंचा" OR तापमान OR "तापमान बढ़ा" OR "रिकॉर्ड तोड़ गर्मी" OR "डिग्री सेल्सियस" OR "पारा उबला" OR "अधिकतम तापमान" OR "तापमान 40 पार" OR "तापमान 45 पार" OR "तापमान बढ़ने की संभावना") Andaman and Nicobar Islands
articles.full_text:
ठंड की गिरफ्त में मध्य प्रदेश, दिवाली के बाद 360 डिग्री बदलेगा मौसम, रात में गिर रहा तापमान
मध्य प्रदेश में बढ़ने लगी है ठंड, इंदौर-भोपाल में ठिठुरन, 10 नवंबर से दिखेगा पश्चिमी विक्षोभ का असर. रिपोर्ट विश्वास चतुर्वेदी.
भोपाल: मध्य प्रदेश में मौसम का मिजाज तेजी से बदल रहा है. दिन में भले ही हल्की गर्मी का अहसास हो रहा हो, लेकिन रात का तापमान गिरने से ठंड का असर बढ़ने लगा है. पिछले 24 घंटों में इंदौर में न्यूनतम तापमान 3.7 डिग्री और भोपाल में 2.7 डिग्री तक लुढ़क गया. वहीं, कई जिलों में रात का तापमान सामान्य से 5 डिग्री तक अधिक बना हुआ है. हालांकि, मौसम के इस उतार-चढ़ाव से सुबह और देर रात ठंड का एहसास बढ़ रहा है. मौसम वैज्ञानिकों के अनुसार 10 नवंबर से एक नया पश्चिमी विक्षोभ पश्चिमी हिमालयी क्षेत्र को प्रभावित कर सकता है, जिसके बाद प्रदेश के मौसम में फिर बदलाव देखने को मिल सकता है.
रात के तापमान में गिरावट, इंदौर-भोपाल में बढ़ी ठिठुरन
मध्य प्रदेश के कई शहरों में रात के तापमान में गिरावट दर्ज की गई है. इंदौर में न्यूनतम तापमान 3.7 डिग्री गिरकर 12.7 डिग्री सेल्सियस पर पहुंच गया. वहीं भोपाल में 2.7 डिग्री की गिरावट के बाद न्यूनतम तापमान 13.5 डिग्री सेल्सियस दर्ज किया गया. इसके अलावा बैतूल, जबलपुर और रायसेन में भी न्यूनतम तापमान में गिरावट दर्ज की गई है.
छिंदवाड़ा में दिन का पारा 4.6 डिग्री चढ़ा
बता दें कि रात में ठंड बढ़ने के बावजूद प्रदेश के कुछ हिस्सों में दिन के तापमान में भी बढ़ोतरी हुई है. छिंदवाड़ा में गुरुवार को अधिकतम तापमान 4.6 डिग्री बढ़कर 35.4 डिग्री सेल्सियस पहुंच गया, जो प्रदेश के प्रमुख केंद्रों में सबसे अधिक रहा. वहीं, भोपाल में भी दिन का तापमान एक डिग्री बढ़कर 31.6 डिग्री सेल्सियस दर्ज किया गया. इसके उलट बैतूल और मलाजखंड में अधिकतम तापमान में क्रमशः 0.7 और 0.9 डिग्री की गिरावट आई है. यानी प्रदेश में दिन और रात के मौसम का अंतर लगातार बढ़ रहा है.

- अर्णब तूफान 1 हजार किमी दूर टकराया, असर मध्य प्रदेश तक कैसे? देर रात से तूफानी बारिश, आज भी ऑरेंज अलर्ट
शिवपुरी-टीकमगढ़ में रात का तापमान सामान्य से ज्यादा
प्रदेश के कुछ जिलों में अभी रात की ठंड का असर अपेक्षाकृत कम है. गुरुवार-शुक्रवार की दरमियानी रात शिवपुरी में न्यूनतम तापमान 21 डिग्री और टीकमगढ़ में 18.2 डिग्री सेल्सियस दर्ज किया गया. इन शहरों का तापमान सामान्य से क्रमशः 5.9 और 5.8 डिग्री अधिक रहा. वहीं, दतिया में भी न्यूनतम तापमान सामान्य से 4.8 डिग्री अधिक दर्ज हुआ. इससे समझाा जा सकता है कि प्रदेश के सभी हिस्सों में ठंड का असर एक जैसा नहीं है.
10 नवंबर से पश्चिमी विक्षोभ का असर
मौसम वैज्ञानिक अरुण शर्मा के अनुसार "वर्तमान में मध्य क्षोभमंडल में पछुआ हवाओं के साथ एक पश्चिमी विक्षोभ सक्रिय है. इसका अक्ष समुद्र तल से करीब 5.8 किलोमीटर की ऊंचाई पर स्थित है. वहीं, 10 नवंबर से एक नया पश्चिमी विक्षोभ पश्चिमी हिमालयी क्षेत्र को प्रभावित कर सकता है. इसके चलते प्रदेश के मौसम में आगे भी बदलाव की संभावना है." शर्मा के अनुसार फिलहाल मध्य प्रदेश के तापमान में उतार-चढ़ाव के बीच सुबह और रात की ठंड बढ़ने के संकेत हैं.

articles.title: When extreme heat becomes a pregnancy risk - Unitaid
articles.search_term: (heatwave OR "heat wave" OR "severe heatwave" OR "extreme heat" OR "heat spell" OR "scorching heat" OR "blistering heat" OR "sweltering heat" OR "hot winds" OR loo OR "hot loo winds" OR "intense heat" OR "unbearable heat" OR "deadly heat" OR heat OR "weather forecast" OR "weather update" OR "weather alert" OR "IMD forecast" OR "IMD prediction" OR "IMD alert" OR IMD OR "rising temperatures" OR "temperatures expected to rise" OR "relief from heat" OR "respite from heat" OR "heat respite" OR "respite from scorching heat") Andaman and Nicobar Islands
articles.full_text:
On a hot day in Kenya, a pregnant woman may face a deceptively simple choice: travel to a health facility in the heat or wait until temperatures fall.
For a woman at risk of preeclampsia, that decision can be critical.
Women will delay coming in, especially when there is extreme heat. Some women, she says, will travel very early in the morning; others may not come at all, preferring to stay somewhere cooler.
Eunice Atsali
Kenyan midwife and Vice President of the Midwives Association of Kenya
When they eventually arrive, they may no longer be seeking routine antenatal care. They may have swelling, severe headaches or other signs of complications. By then, their placenta may already be impaired, and the baby may need to be delivered urgently.
This is not simply a question of discomfort. A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis covering 28 studies and more than 23 million pregnancies found that heat exposure was associated with a 58% higher risk of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy. The odds of pre-eclampsia were approximately doubled, while each 1°C increase in temperature was associated with a 3% increase in the odds of hypertensive disorders.
The findings do not mean heat directly causes every case of pre-eclampsia. But they add to growing evidence that rising temperatures pose a serious threat to maternal health. Extreme heat during pregnancy has also been associated with higher risks of stillbirth and neonatal death. Behind every pregnant woman exposed to extreme heat is a developing fetus, potentially vulnerable to the same changing conditions.
The findings overall strengthen the case for making maternal health systems more resilient to heat – particularly as extreme temperatures become more common.
Romane Theoleyre, Programme Manager at Unitaid, puts it succinctly: “Because the biggest risk is not only more cases. It’s delayed and missed care.”
Preeclampsia can be life-threatening, but early detection and appropriate management can reduce the risks to mother and baby. The problem is that climate change can undermine the entire pathway from prevention and antenatal screening to diagnosis, treatment and emergency referral.
Pregnancy already places additional demands on the body. Extreme heat adds physiological stress, while climate-related pressures such as food insecurity, water scarcity and infectious disease can compound existing vulnerabilities.
For women, getting to care may become harder just when they need it most. Flooding can cut off roads and delay emergency referrals. Drought can worsen nutrition and maternal anemia. Extreme heat can make long journeys and waits at exposed clinics physically demanding.
And the facilities they are trying to reach may be struggling too.
Eunice describes maternity wards where midwives work 12-hour shifts caring for large numbers of women without reliable access to drinking water. Dehydration and exhaustion can undermine their ability to provide safe, attentive care.
“There’s a high likelihood you’re actually going to forget even giving basic care management to the women,” she says.
In maternal healthcare, the women facing these risks are often caring for other women. Climate pressures can therefore affect both sides of the care equation: pregnant women trying to access services and the health workers responsible for delivering them.
Climate change is making an already demanding job harder for health workers and an already vulnerable period more dangerous for women. And the challenge will intensify as temperatures rise. Climate projections for Kenya point to a future of greater heat exposure, making it increasingly important for health services to prepare for conditions that existing infrastructure and systems may not have been designed to withstand.
Stéphanie Mariat, Climate & Health Officer at Unitaid, describes climate change as a “structural” issue for maternal health. She says, “It affects the risks women face, their ability to seek care and the capacity of health services to respond.”
For Unitaid, addressing these challenges also means ensuring that climate resilience is considered in the health products people depend on so that medicines, diagnostics and devices remain accessible and effective as climate conditions change.
That is particularly important in low- and middle-income countries, where communities may face greater exposure to climate hazards while having fewer resources to protect themselves.
The response does not necessarily begin with expensive new technology. It starts with ensuring that health workers have the basic tools they need to prevent, identify and manage pre-eclampsia – and that those tools remain available and reliable in increasingly challenging conditions.
Stéphanie explains: “For preeclampsia, adaptation may start with making sure that proven tools – from blood pressure monitoring devices to diagnostics and treatment commodities – remain available and functional, even in challenging climatic conditions.”
Take low-dose aspirin, one of the most affordable, effective and available interventions for lowering the risk of preeclampsia. Aspirin can degrade over time, especially when exposed to high heat and humidity. Similarly, magnesium sulfate, used to prevent and treat the life-threatening seizures that can occur in women with severe preeclampsia, has specific storage recommendations to avoid high temperatures and humidity.

articles.title: How FCT residents cope with scorching heat as the rainy season bows out - Blueprint Newspapers
articles.search_term: (heatwave OR "heat wave" OR "severe heatwave" OR "extreme heat" OR "heat spell" OR "scorching heat" OR "blistering heat" OR "sweltering heat" OR "hot winds" OR loo OR "hot loo winds" OR "intense heat" OR "unbearable heat" OR "deadly heat" OR heat OR "weather forecast" OR "weather update" OR "weather alert" OR "IMD forecast" OR "IMD prediction" OR "IMD alert" OR IMD OR "rising temperatures" OR "temperatures expected to rise" OR "relief from heat" OR "respite from heat" OR "heat respite" OR "respite from scorching heat") Andaman and Nicobar Islands
articles.full_text:
Scorching heat has become the order of the day in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) and indeed across the country as the rainy season recedes for the year, forcing residents to seek solution; PAUL OKAH reports.
The rainy season is already saying its ‘byes’ for this year, while the dry season is gearing up to take its place. And with the final rainfall to herald the coming of the North-easterly trade wind, popularly known as harmattan, not forthcoming, scorching heat has become the order of the day forcing FCT residents to sweat excessively.
To make matters worse, there is the ever-stubborn epileptic power supply across the Territory’s towns. Hence, residents are now grateful if they get power supply for up to 30 minutes or one hour in a day to mitigate the heat.
Residents’ ordeals
A Bwari-based businessman, Clement Opeyemi, said he spends much time under trees in his compound to mitigate the scorching heat.
He said, “The heat is too much nowadays. Rain has ceased in different places, so the heat is naturally coming with the dry season. It’s especially felt if you’re outside doing one thing or the other, unlike when you’re indoors. The heat may not be felt until when the sun comes out.
“I planted trees in my compound when I was building my house. So, once there is no light and the heat is too much inside, I simply take my bath and sit under the trees with my wife. It’s there I’ll have my dinner and rest. It’s one of the advantages of one having your own house.
“So, if you can’t afford to run your generator because of the cost of fuelling it or if you don’t have a solar energy facility, the best thing is just to stay outside for a while to get a fresh breeze before going inside.
“Once you can take your bath regularly, the heat will reduce. It’s especially good if you tiled your floor because you won’t feel much heat if you take your bath and lie on the tiled floor.”
Also, a civil servant, Amina Yusuf, said the excessive heat has forced her to become reluctant in going to work or stressing herself while at home, adding that she takes her bath regularly to mitigate the scorching heat.
She said, “To be honest with you, the heat is too much and I am beginning to miss the rainy season. Imagine a situation whereby you can’t walk from one point to another without sweating profusely because of the scorching heat. It’s making life unbearable as my clothes are always soaked once I’m outside the house.
“Nevertheless, if I’m at home and there’s no light, I always take my bath sometimes every three or four hours. Then I’ll lie on the tiled floor in wrappers. It’s those who have solar facilities that enjoy their time because the sun is important and their AC or fans will be switched on, but they will still feel the heat once they’re outside their comfort zones. Honestly, I can’t wait for the harmattan to start.”
On his part, a student in Lugbe, James Abdullahi, said the heat has been intolerable, especially as there has not been power supply in his area for over a week.
He said, “Those people enjoying steady power supply may not know what God has done for them. The heat has just been too much. It’s as if someone opened the door of hell and forgot to close it. Just stepping out of your house to get something on the street in the afternoon would be asking for trouble as you will surely be drenched in sweat when you come back from the sun.
“That said, what I’ve been doing since the onset of the hot weather is to wear lighter clothes while leaving my house for anything. But if I am inside the house, I bathe at intervals. Even if it’s without soap, I just pour the water on my body without even drying up. Then I’ll put on only my boxers. Since I’m staying alone, I don’t inconvenience anyone with my dressing or anything. Also, when the heat becomes too much, I apply powder on my body after bathing.
“The trick I learned from my mum is that powder absorbs sweat. So, once I finish taking my bath, I would allow the water to dry a little on my body and then apply powder to absorb sweat. That way, I’ll stay for a long time without feeling heat. It’s especially when I am outside the house that I sweat a lot.”
An expert’s admonition
Speaking with Blueprint Weekend, a nutritionist, Mrs. Philomena Okeke, advised FCT residents to always stay hydrated, saying the scorching heat can be mitigated using a combination of several factors.
She said, “To survive the scorching heat in the FCT, residents must prioritise deep hydration. As a resident, modify your daily outdoor schedule and ensure adequate cooling. The FCT and other parts of the country experience intense heat waves, particularly during the transition months, making heat management essential for health and safety.
“Therefore, residents must stay hydrated. Drink water constantly. Do not wait until you are thirsty; carry a reusable water bottle everywhere and drink at least 3 to 4 liters daily. Consume drinks like coconut water, Kunu or water with a pinch of salt and lemon to replace minerals lost through heavy sweating.
“People should also consume smaller, more frequent meals high in water content—such as watermelon, cucumbers and oranges – while avoiding heavy, protein-rich foods that increase metabolic heat. People should also try and limit dehydrating drinks. Avoid excessive caffeine, sugary soft drinks and alcohol as they cause your body to lose fluids faster.”
Continuing, she said, “Also, dressing matters. People should wear loose, light-colored clothing. Choose breathable fabrics like cotton or linen that allow air circulation and reflect heat rather than absorbing it. Always wear a wide-brimmed hat, UV-blocking sunglasses and carry an umbrella when walking under direct sunlight. If you can, avoid going outdoors to prevent severe sunburn.
“If you’re indoors, maximise ventilation. Keep windows open during early mornings and evenings when the air is cooler and close curtains or blinds during peak afternoon hours to block out radiant heat. From experience, the public grid can be unreliable during peak heat periods, so ensure your backup power sources (inverters, solar or generators) are prepared to run fans or air conditioning.
“If you’re using a vehicle, purge trapped car heat. Open all car doors for a few minutes to let trapped, superheated air escape before turning on the vehicle’s air conditioner. More importantly, never leave anyone in a parked vehicle. Yes, do not leave children, pets or vulnerable individuals inside a parked car for any duration as temperatures reach lethal levels within minutes during the heat period.”

articles.title: HEATWAVE AND PREGNANCY: 2024 heat linked to preterm births in Western Visayas, Negros - Daily Guardian
articles.search_term: (heatwave OR "heat wave" OR "severe heatwave" OR "extreme heat" OR "heat spell" OR "scorching heat" OR "blistering heat" OR "sweltering heat" OR "hot winds" OR loo OR "hot loo winds" OR "intense heat" OR "unbearable heat" OR "deadly heat" OR heat OR "weather forecast" OR "weather update" OR "weather alert" OR "IMD forecast" OR "IMD prediction" OR "IMD alert" OR IMD OR "rising temperatures" OR "temperatures expected to rise" OR "relief from heat" OR "respite from heat" OR "heat respite" OR "respite from scorching heat") Andaman and Nicobar Islands
articles.full_text:
Extreme heat in April 2024 was linked to an estimated 28 excess preterm births in Western Visayas and 27 in the Negros Island Region, according to a new analysis by Zero Carbon Analytics (ZCA).
Those were the highest counts among the Visayas regions. Central Visayas followed with 23 and Eastern Visayas with 16.
Together, the Visayas regions accounted for 94 excess preterm births, or 16% of the national total.
Nationwide, the heat was linked to an estimated 10% rise in preterm births compared with a typical April. That equals 585 excess preterm births during the 15-day heat event from April 15 to 29, 2024, or around 8 per 1,000 births.
Calabarzon had the most excess preterm births at 103, followed by Metro Manila and Central Luzon. Metro Manila accounted for 82, or 14% of the national total.
Cagayan Valley in northern Luzon had both the largest increase in preterm birth risk, around 15%, and the highest rate, at 12 per 1,000 births. Cagayan province was 4.01 degrees Celsius hotter than normal, and its risk rose by 17%. Caraga in Mindanao had the lowest rate, at 3 per 1,000 births.
During the heat event, the average person in the Philippines experienced temperatures 2.44 degrees Celsius above normal.
ZCA said its regional figures can show where more health service capacity may be needed, including adding heat protection to prenatal care, community maternal health services, and health-system preparedness.
The research group also estimated that 263 preterm births in the Philippines during the April 2024 heat would not have occurred without human-caused climate change.
According to World Weather Attribution (WWA), the heat the Philippines experienced would have been virtually impossible without human-caused climate change. WWA also found that climate change made the heat about 1.2 degrees Celsius hotter in the Philippines.
At 7.7%, the Philippines has a lower preterm birth rate than India or Bangladesh, but its heat exposure has risen the fastest of the three countries.
ZCA cited a May 2025 analysis by Climate Central, which found that climate change caused 30 of the 36 pregnancy heat-risk days the Philippines had each year from 2020 to 2024. That is 83% of the total.
The Philippines ranked seventh in Germanwatch’s Climate Risk Index 2026. India ranked 15th and Bangladesh 13th. ZCA said pregnancy-specific heat exposure in these countries is rising faster than almost anywhere else in the world.
ZCA said it found no heat-specific maternal health guideline or heat action plan for the Philippines.
The country’s Maternal, Newborn, Child Health and Nutrition strategy aims to reduce maternal and newborn deaths through health services. However, ZCA said it was not designed with heat in mind.
The World Health Organization defines preterm birth as the birth of a live infant before 37 full weeks of pregnancy. It is the leading cause of newborn deaths worldwide and is associated with long-term physical, neurodevelopmental, and socioeconomic effects for babies.
Across the Philippines, India, and Bangladesh, ZCA estimated that human-caused climate change caused 10,600 excess preterm births during the April 2024 heatwave alone. The 95% confidence interval runs from 5,100 to 17,700.
Of that total, around 8,830 were in India, 1,479 in Bangladesh, and 263 in the Philippines. These are births that would not have occurred without human-caused warming.
According to WWA, human-caused climate change made the April 2024 heat event around 45 times more likely in South Asia and about 0.85 degrees Celsius hotter there.
In a separate analysis, ZCA compared April 2024 with a typical April. April is already one of the hottest months of the year in the three countries. By that measure, the heat was associated with roughly 16,150 excess preterm births, with a 95% confidence interval of 10,100 to 22,400.
That included a 3.6% increase in preterm births in India, an 11.9% increase in Bangladesh, and a 10% increase in the Philippines.
ZCA said the 10,600 figure is not a share of the 16,150 figure. The 16,150 figure compares the event with the climate of the past three decades, which already includes much of the warming so far. The 10,600 figure compares it with a world without human-caused climate change.
South Asia had the highest preterm birth rate of any region in 2020, at 13.2%. That year, Bangladesh had the highest average rate of any country at 16.2%, with little improvement over the past decade. India’s rate was 13.0%.
The analysis drew on temperature data, preterm birth data, attribution science, and advanced climate models. ZCA said it is the first study to estimate how many preterm births in the three countries were linked to the April 2024 heat, including where the burden fell within each country.
ZCA said it is also the first study to estimate how many of those births can be attributed to human-caused climate change. It also projects how continued global warming could affect preterm births in India and Bangladesh by the middle of the century.
The group said some of the preterm births it counted may not be additional overall, because heat can bring forward a birth that would have been preterm anyway. It added that its results may underestimate the burden from humid heat.
The study found that maternal health policies and heat action plans do not yet consistently protect pregnant women and babies from heat in the Philippines, India, or Bangladesh.
The researchers said better prenatal care, access to cooling, and early warning systems are needed to reduce some of the preterm births caused by climate change.
Exposure to extreme heat during pregnancy is also linked to higher risks of hypertension, gestational diabetes, severe maternal illness, and stillbirth. Droughts, floods, and air pollution from burning fossil fuels pose additional and growing threats to the health of mothers and newborns in the region.
The findings come during another year of unprecedented heatwaves and other extreme weather fueled by climate change, with global warming also strengthening the current El Niño.
COP31 opens next week, and health is among its key priorities. Ahead of the conference, the U.N. climate chief launched a call to address how climate-driven heat affects pregnancy and birth, describing it as “a new faultline in the global climate crisis, and one which is potentially fatal.”
The U.N. climate chief also cited a September 2026 Wellcome Trust survey of 1,000 maternal health care workers in five countries, including India. Seventy-three percent said they had seen more heat-related cases or complications among pregnant women over the past five years. Ninety-two percent said they wanted more training and resources to protect them.
The WHO, the World Meteorological Organization, UNICEF, and UNFPA also recently launched a global framework to track the growing health risks of extreme heat for pregnant women, newborns, and children.
The 2026 Report of the Lancet Countdown on Health and Climate Change, published Oct. 28, 2026, found that many health impacts of climate change are outpacing climate action. It called for climate change to be declared a global health emergency.
Dr. Joanne Bentley-McKune, the report’s lead author and a senior research analyst at ZCA, said: “Climate change is making extreme heat more frequent and intense, raising the risk of preterm birth, which is linked to lifelong health impacts.”
“Our research estimates that the extreme heat of April 2024 may have caused more than 16,000 additional preterm births in India, Bangladesh and the Philippines, compared with a typical April in recent decades. Compared with a world without human-caused climate change, we estimate that more than 10,000 of that month’s preterm births would not have occurred,” she said.
“These impacts will grow as temperatures rise: we project that by mid-century, an ordinary April in India could see even more additional preterm births than the exceptionally hot April of 2024,” Bentley-McKune added.
ZCA projected that for 2041 to 2060, a typical April could bring roughly 15,300 excess preterm births in India, with a 95% range of 6,800 to 28,100. For Bangladesh, the projection is roughly 1,500, with a range of 630 to 2,900. Both figures are compared with an average April from 1985 to 2014 and assume no adaptation measures.
Bentley-McKune also warned about El Niño: “Moreover, an exceptionally strong El Niño is currently forecast to still be in place when the 2027 pre-monsoon season begins, so the coming season could bring another period of extreme heat to South and Southeast Asia. Our findings show that extreme heat can lead to more preterm births, which have severe health risks. Heat protection needs to be in place before it arrives to protect mothers and babies.”
“The countries analysed have contributed relatively little to the historical emissions driving climate change, yet are disproportionately affected by climate-driven extreme weather compared with high-income, high-emitting countries, which also have more resources to adapt,” she said.
“Our estimates can help identify where greater health service capacity is needed, and adaptation measures – such as better antenatal care and early warning systems – should be prioritised. However, these could prevent only some of the preterm birth burden imposed by climate change, so limiting further warming remains crucial,” Bentley-McKune said.
Dr. Rashmi Agarwalla reviewed the briefing. She is the nodal officer for climate change and an associate professor in the Department of Community and Family Medicine at AIIMS Guwahati. She said: “Climate change is a public health emergency, and pregnant women and their babies are on the frontline, particularly in highly climate-vulnerable countries such as India, Bangladesh and the Philippines.”
“As a doctor working in India, emerging evidence suggests that extreme heat disproportionately affects pregnant women and newborns. Anemia, poor nutrition, and prolonged outdoor work further compound these risks, particularly in vulnerable communities. Yet, heat remains an often-overlooked threat to maternal and neonatal health within our healthcare systems,” Agarwalla said.
The release said the analysis should remind governments that, as temperatures rise, protecting mothers from heat must become a routine part of health-system preparedness, prenatal care, and community maternal health services.
It also urged governments to phase out fossil fuels and to increase international climate finance for developing countries, which would fund both adaptation and emission-reduction measures.

articles.full_text:
The National Meteorological Service (SMN) has issued yellow alerts in several Argentine provinces for this Friday, November 6, warning of potential severe weather conditions such as strong storms, wind, and the Zonda phenomenon. These weather events could cause significant damage and disrupt daily activities. Weather alerts allow citizens to prepare in advance and take preventive measures to minimize personal and material risks.
Affected provinces by storms and Zonda wind
In the City of Buenos Aires, no weather alerts have been activated, but showers are anticipated during the morning and afternoon with a 70% chance of rain. At night, isolated storms are likely to occur with a 100% chance of precipitation. Although there are no alerts, citizens should stay informed about the weather to avoid surprises and ensure they have a plan in case conditions worsen.
The SMN’s Early Warning System has issued a storm warning for the provinces of Buenos Aires, La Pampa, and San Luis. These storms could bring precipitation of between 15 and 40 millimeters, as well as hail, strong gusts, and electrical activity. Severe storms can cause local flooding and property damage, highlighting the importance of preparedness measures. Rapid water accumulation in urban areas can significantly affect infrastructure and mobility, so it is crucial that local authorities and citizens work together to reduce these risks.
The agency recommends staying indoors, not taking out the trash, and ensuring that drains and gutters are clear. It is advisable to disconnect appliances and cut off the power supply if water enters the home. If outdoors, seeking shelter quickly is essential. These precautions help mitigate the material and personal damage that storms can cause. Coordination with emergency services and compliance with instructions can make a significant difference in reducing negative impacts.
Impact of strong winds and the Zonda
In addition to storms, alerts for strong winds have been issued for the provinces of Catamarca, La Rioja, Santiago del Estero, Córdoba, La Pampa, Mendoza, and San Luis. Mountainous regions are expected to experience winds of between 45 and 70 km/h with gusts exceeding 110 km/h. Intense winds can cause trees and power lines to fall, posing a danger to public safety. Communities must be prepared for possible interruptions in the supply of essential services and cooperate with authorities to ensure their safety.
Finally, the Zonda wind phenomenon will affect La Rioja, Tucumán, San Juan, Catamarca, and Mendoza. Speeds of between 30 and 50 km/h with gusts exceeding 70 km/h are expected. This phenomenon can reduce visibility and cause a sudden increase in temperatures. The Zonda wind is known for its ability to dry the environment, which can worsen the situation of forest fires in the affected regions. The population should be especially attentive to the instructions of the authorities to prevent fires and protect natural resources.
In conclusion, the alerts issued by the SMN highlight the importance of preparation for extreme weather events. Citizens should stay alert to weather updates and follow safety recommendations to protect themselves and their property. Timely information and following instructions can help effectively manage the adverse situations that these weather phenomena may cause.
